newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coffee roasters reluctantly follow market.
newsitem.headline: German coffee roasters reluctantly follow market.

text.p: Firmer outright coffee prices as a result of last week's futures upturn were unwelcome but roasters had grudgingly followed the market higher, German traders said on Monday.
New York arabicas made sharp gains after a surprising drawdown in U.S. certified stocks and a cautious Brazil government crop forecast for 1997/98, which increased supply fears.
New York March gained 3.35 cents on the week, nearly three percent, and last stood at 119.60.
Some traders saw the position poised for gains up to 125.
"Consumers don't like high origin and afloat prices but they have accepted higher prices ex-local stocks," one trader said.
"They are even accepting very firm East African prices if they need the coffee in their blends."
A firm dollar was also adding to the costs of mark buyers.
Robusta prices were seen coming under supply pressure, which could widen the discount to arabicas, but they play a very minor role in traditional German blends.
Differentials on arabicas were expected to hold firm over the next few weeks as origin shippers were seen marking up and retaining desirable qualities.
Importers reported roaster enquiries for March/April and June/July, with interest focused on cheap Central Americans and second hands.
Arabica prices were up $10-19 per 50 kg fob from pre-Christmas levels.
Brazils were at $129 second hand and $133 ex-origin compared with $115-120 asked for afloat lots last week.
Vietnamese robustas grade 2 were at $52 cif.
Traders believed the Brazil crop estimate of 18.5-19.5 million 60-kg bags versus 25 million in 1996/97 was too low and too early to cause serious concern.
"It comes from the same circles that were too low at the same time last year," one trader said.
Roaster sentiment was depressed as there was no sign lower retail prices carried over from 1996 could be reversed, and this should further erode already slim operating margins.
